title: Beautifying a mitzvah
hook: lovely candlesticks, a fine cup, a hand-made challah cover
tomorrow: the custom nobody remembers starting. what's yours?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judah ibn Tibbon's bookcases as gardens. Books at home. Today, from the shelf to the table: the things you hold while you bless.

People spend an hour choosing the right font for a birthday card that gets read once. The Kiddush blessing works the same over a paper cup as over a silver one. So why does the tradition bother with a beautiful cup at all? One question for today: does beauty matter to God?
screen: `AN HOUR ON THE FONT.` → `PAPER CUP OR SILVER?` → `DOES BEAUTY MATTER TO GOD?`

segments.voice: The rabbis start from one line of the song at the sea: "This is my God, and I will glorify Him." The Talmud, in Shabbat, reads glorify as adorn: make yourself beautiful before God in mitzvot. A beautiful sukkah, a beautiful shofar, a Torah scroll written in fine ink with a fine pen by a skilled scribe. The name is hiddur mitzvah, beautifying a commandment. The Talmud even sets a measure: for hiddur mitzvah, spend up to a third more. So the tradition's answer is yes, with a limit. Beauty doesn't make the blessing work. It says the blessing matters. Polished candlesticks on Friday afternoon. A hand-made challah cover. And a neighbor says something close. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says God is beautiful and loves beauty. Jews and Muslims both hold that beauty and God belong together. One honest difference. In the hadith, the line answers a man worried that liking fine clothes and shoes is pride: beauty in how a person presents themselves isn't arrogance. In the Talmud, the beauty goes into the objects of a commandment: the cup, the scroll, the sukkah. Both make room for beauty. They place it in different spots.
screen: `THIS IS MY GOD, I WILL GLORIFY HIM.` · `ADORN THE MITZVAH: CUP, SCROLL, SUKKAH.` · `UP TO A THIRD MORE.` · `GOD IS BEAUTIFUL AND LOVES BEAUTY.` · then, large: `BEAUTIFUL MITZVOT.`

segments.voice: Pick up one object you use for something that matters to you: a cup, a candleholder, a pen, a bowl. Wipe it slowly with a cloth or your sleeve until it shines a little. Then set it down somewhere it can be seen.
screen: `ONE OBJECT THAT MATTERS.` · `WIPE IT SLOWLY.` · `SET IT WHERE IT'S SEEN.`

segments.voice: Hiddur mitzvah: beautifying a commandment, from this is my God, and I will glorify Him. The cup matters because of what's said over it.
Pocket it: beautiful mitzvot, a cup or a candlestick polished on a Friday afternoon. Fourteen of fifteen, shining.

chat.says: made a challah cover for benny's shabbat. took 4 hours, still crooked. pointless if the bread's the same?
options: Not pointless. Hiddur mitzvah: beauty says this matters. Hand-made, crooked, counts.
Kind of. A mitzvah's beauty only counts if it's flawless and costly.
Yes. God cares about the blessing, so the cover is just decoration.
chat.meaning: The Talmud reads 'I will glorify Him' as adorning a mitzvah. The beauty is in the care, not the price or perfection.
